about.title: Chino Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Chino is a city of roughly 85,600 people in the western corner of San Bernardino County, and most residents get their care close to home before being referred elsewhere for anything complex. When something goes wrong along that path — a scan read too quickly, a medication mixed up at discharge, a surgery that leaves damage no one warned you about — it can be hard to tell whether you experienced ordinary bad luck or actual negligence. California draws that line carefully. Under MICRA, a poor result by itself is not malpractice; a qualified medical expert almost always has to explain how the care fell below the accepted standard. The clock is short, too: generally one year from when you discovered the harm, and never more than three years from the injury, with a 90-day notice sent to the provider before any lawsuit is filed. We handle medical malpractice claims on a contingency basis, so having your records reviewed costs nothing upfront.

items.title: We respect MICRA's short window
items.desc: Malpractice claims in California generally must be brought within one year of discovering the injury and never more than three years from when it occurred. We move quickly so the 90-day pre-suit notice can go out in time.

items.title: Our team works with medical experts
items.desc: A qualified medical expert is almost always required to show the standard of care was breached. We know how to line that up early.

items.title: Honest about what counts as malpractice
items.desc: A bad outcome alone is not negligence, and we won't pretend otherwise. We will tell you plainly whether the facts support a claim, with no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was treated after a crash on SR-60 in Chino and the hospital missed a fracture. Is that a malpractice case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It may be both, and they are handled as separate claims. The driver who caused the collision is responsible for the crash injuries, while a provider who failed to diagnose a fracture that a reasonable physician would have caught may be responsible for the added harm. We can sort out which party owes what and keep both sets of deadlines straight.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover in a California malpractice claim?
items.answer: California places a statutory cap on non-economic damages, meaning pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life. That cap rises each year under current law, so the figure depends on when your case resolves. Economic losses such as medical bills and lost income are not subject to that cap.

items.question: How do I know whether my Chino doctor actually did something wrong?
items.answer: You usually can't know from the outside, and neither can we without the records. The question is whether the care fell below what a competent provider in the same field would have done, and a qualified medical expert nearly always has to answer that. Requesting your complete chart from the facility is a sensible first step, and we can review it at no cost.
